title: P0 Hosted API — soft degradation detection & fallback playbook (draft)
content:
Summary:

This document captures the P0 incident on 2027-01-14 where the Hosted API experienced a prolonged 'soft degradation' — elevated p95/p99 latencies and intermittent streaming stalls — for ~37 minutes across two regions. There were few hard 5xx spikes, so automated escalation and fallbacks did not trigger reliably. This doc is a synthesis of timeline, on-call notes, immediate mitigations, root-cause hypotheses, and concrete runbook/playbook changes we should adopt to reduce time-to-mitigate for similar future incidents.

High-level impact:
- Timespan: 2027-01-14 17:12:00 UTC -> 17:49:00 UTC (37m total; partial recovery by 17:42 with gradual normalization)
- Affected customers: multiple PLG customers observed elevated latency and partial streaming truncation; 3 paying accounts reported degraded UX/slow responses; no data loss reported.
- SLOs: p99 latency exceeded 5s target, p95 exceeded 2s for majority of the window.
- Symptoms: slow initial token generation, intermittent streaming token gaps (small pauses), some client reconnects.

Timeline (consolidated from traces/logs/Slack/oncall notes):
- 17:11:25 UTC: small increase in prefix-cache eviction rates from edge hosts (metric: kv_cache.eviction_rate spike).
- 17:12:00 UTC: alerts for p95 latency in us-west (alert: hostedapi-p95-latency-high) start firing. Pager routed to on-call SRE and serving-runtime owner.
- 17:12:40 UTC: first customer message in support channel; some clients report partial streaming stalls and reconnects.
- 17:14:00 UTC: tracing shows increased time spent in assemble_response step (runtime) and higher queue depth on cross-tenant batcher.
- 17:17:00 UTC: minor bump in CPU on inference gateway proxies; autoscaler did not trigger due to short window.
- 17:20:00 UTC: mitigation attempt — temporary increase of per-route concurrency cap on edge routers (manual) to relieve portal queuing. Small improvement but p95 still high.
- 17:26:00 UTC: investigation reveals a simultaneous small change in load routing policy (canary flag rollout) that shifted a subset of high-Latency prefixes to a new routing slab with different cache-locality characteristics.
- 17:31:00 UTC: team performs targeted prefix warmup (replay of cached prefixes) to repopulate KV caches on affected slab. Latency improves gradually.
- 17:42:00 UTC: streaming gaps reduced; p95 trending down but still above target.
- 17:49:00 UTC: p95/p99 return to normal baseline. Post-incident triage begins.

Immediate mitigations performed (on-call):
- Raised edge per-route concurrency caps to prevent queue head-of-line blocking. (owner: oncall-sre)
- Rolled back the routing canary flag to previous slab for affected tenant traffic. (owner: release-engineering)
- Manual prefix warmup script executed for the new slab to repopulate KV caches (owner: serving-runtime)
- Customer comms: brief status message posted to support channel; follow-up email to impacted accounts. (owner: customer-success)

Root cause analysis (hypothesis with evidence):
Primary contributors: cache-locality regression triggered by routing-canary rollout + insufficient quick-fallback logic for soft degradations.
- The routing policy change (canary) moved a slice of traffic that had high prefix overlap into a slab where KV cache size and priming state were different. Evidence: cross-correlation of request prefixes with cache miss rates spiking on new slab hosts at 17:11–17:14 UTC.
- The runtime's batcher aggregated more requests that had higher cold-kv miss rates, increasing per-request latency (assemble_response waiting on KV fetch).
- Fallback logic only triggers on hard errors / 5xx or host unreachability; it does not currently trigger on sustained p95/p99 latency anomalies at the per-route granularity. This meant the automated router did not shift traffic away during the slow window.

Secondary factors: small autoscaler hysteresis and short burst window meant node pools did not scale quickly enough; edge concurrency caps were conservative and created head-of-line queuing under the transient load pattern.

Why was it a P0 (not P1)?
- Short window but broad user-facing impact across multiple customers and triggered customer escalations. The lack of automatic fallback and slow mitigations required manual intervention from multiple teams.

On-call notes (raw, taken during incident):
- "17:13 — cache miss rate weird, multiple prefixes thrashing" — Rafael
- "17:21 — canary flag rollback reduces N1 queue depth a bit" — Tanya
- "17:28 — warmup script seems to help; need longer-term priming after slab changes" — Devon
- "17:33 — support reports streaming gaps quieter; still watching p99" — Marta

Gaps identified in current runbook and systems:
1) No per-route latency-based automated fallback. Existing fallbacks rely on 5xx/unhealthy signaling.
2) KV cache priming/rehydration after routing slab changes is manual and slow.
3) Alerts are noisy and not grouped by route-model-prefix; tracing is available but slow to triage under pressure.
4) Edge concurrency defaults can produce head-of-line blocking for mixed short/long requests.

Immediate action items (P0 -> short term, owners and due dates):
- (ASAP, 7d) Implement a short-circuit detection in router: if p95 for a route exceeds X for Y duration, mark route as degraded and route to fallback slab/model variant. (owner: serving-runtime) — JIRA-INF-9041
- (ASAP, 3d) Add a pre-warm hook to routing slab activation: after enabling a slab for traffic, proactively run the existing warmup script against top-N prefixes for that tenant slab. (owner: release-engineering)
- (ASAP, 2d) Update SRE runbook with play-by-play for soft degradation (new doc section) — include exact dashboards, required Slack channels, and rollback steps. (owner: eng-sre)
- (ASAP, 7d) Tweak edge per-route concurrency defaults and expose a per-route override knob in the console for emergency adjustments. (owner: platform-engineering)
- (ASAP, 14d) Instrument a per-prefix latency histogram and an aggregated route health score to enable automated decisions. (owner: observability)

Longer-term countermeasures (roadmap):
- Automatic route health-based traffic steering (policy engine) with configurable SLO thresholds and cool-downs.
- Faster slab activation flow: background priming + proactive model shard cache population.
- Improve autoscaler responsiveness for short transients (burst mode) with sub-minute scale-up options for hot pools.
- Revisit batching heuristics to detect cold-kv batches and prioritize fetching KV shards in parallel.

Runbook draft: (to be inserted into SRE runbook, condensed steps for first responder)
1) Acknowledge alert; post incident channel with region and alert name.
2) Check per-route p95/p99 dashboards and identify if degradation is route-localized or global.
3) Check kv_cache.eviction_rate, kv_cache.miss_rate, and slab activation events for last 30m.
4) If slab activation or routing changes occurred in last 15m, consider rollback of routing canary as first mitigation.
5) Increase edge per-route concurrency cap temporarily and monitor queue depth.
6) Trigger prefix warmup script on affected slab(s) (safe idempotent).
7) If p95 remains > threshold after 10 minutes, open P0 and engage release-engineering + serving-runtime for rollback or targeted traffic migration.
8) Notify customer-success for potential customer comms.

Post-incident owners and deadlines (concrete):
- Serving-runtime: implement per-route latency fallback prototype (due 2027-01-22). owner: Rafael Gomez
- Release-engineering: add slab pre-warm hook and document canary rollback checklist (due 2027-01-22). owner: Tanya Singh
- Observability: add per-prefix latency histogram and alert refinement (due 2027-02-01). owner: Marta Kowalska
- Platform-engineering: expose emergency per-route concurrency override (due 2027-01-29). owner: Devon Lee

Customer communications:
- Support sent a brief incident notification on 2027-01-14 announcing degraded performance and that root cause investigation was underway. Follow-up to impacted customers planned after RCA and remediation timeline confirmed. (owner: customer-success)

Open questions for follow-up triage meeting:
- What threshold (absolute and relative) should mark a route as degraded vs. noisy transient?
- How to safely warm caches without striking new load patterns that can create overload?
- Should we prioritize making the router smarter or the runtime more cache-resilient first?

Appendix: quick links & artifacts (for triage)
- Grafana dashboard: hostedapi-route-latency-overview (link internal)
- Trace sample: trace-id 7a2f1c10 (collected from 17:13–17:21)
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pulls/4526 (warmup helper script)
- Jira: JIRA-INF-9041 (route-fallback), JIRA-RE-1179 (slab-prewarm)

Version notes: this is initial draft of post-incident playbook. Please annotate and add missing fragments from your on-call notes. We will schedule a 60-minute triage + action prioritization meeting on 2027-01-19 to finalize owners and embed the runbook changes into the official SRE runbook page.
